scenario: A requester asks procurement to set up a new vendor immediately. They also offer to create the vendor record themselves to save time.
question: What does the SOP say?

options.text: The person who requests or negotiates with a vendor should not create the vendor record, and a second person should review new vendors and bank changes.
Let the requester create the record since they know the vendor best.
Create the record and approve payment from the same account for speed.

why: Segregation of duties protects the vendor master file, which is a prime target for fraud.

scenario: An email from a vendor asks to change its bank account and includes a new phone number to confirm.
question: How do you verify it?

options.text: Call back using a phone number you have verified independently, never one from the request, and never accept bank changes on email alone.
Call the number in the email, since it is the vendor's own.
Update the bank account if the email signature looks correct.

why: Bank detail changes by email are a classic fraud route. Independent call-back to a known contact is the control.

scenario: A department wants to buy office supplies. Another wants a cloud provider that will hold customer data.
question: How should due diligence differ?

options.text: Tier vendors by risk. Low-tier vendors get basic identity and tax documents, while high-tier vendors get security and privacy review, legal review, executive approval and ongoing monitoring.
Apply the same full review to every vendor, to be safe.
Apply only a quick check to both, since speed matters.

why: One-size-fits-all either slows the business or understates real risks. Tiering keeps scrutiny proportionate.

scenario: A contract auto-renews unless notice is given. The notice window opens next month and nobody has it on a calendar.
question: What should the procedure have done?

options.text: Record key dates such as renewal and review dates at go-live, track renewals and decide well before notice deadlines.
Rely on the vendor to remind you.
Wait until the invoice arrives, then decide.

why: Auto-renewals trap companies in unwanted commitments. Contract management is part of ongoing monitoring.

scenario: A vendor relationship ends after two years.
question: What does offboarding include?

options.text: Give notice per the contract, revoke access, retrieve or confirm deletion of your data, settle invoices and deactivate the vendor in the master file so no further payments can be made.
Stop using their service. Nothing else is required.
Keep their access active in case you need them again.

why: Dormant access and active vendor records linger as risks. Offboarding closes them deliberately.
